introduction: This intermediate tier transitions into the vital components that validate or vitiate (invalidate) a contract. It explores the rules of consideration, the capacity of minors to contract, and the five flaws that destroy free consent.

core_concepts.title: Consideration (Section 2(d))
core_concepts.description:
Consideration is 'Quid Pro Quo' (something in return). A contract without consideration is void (Sec 25), with few exceptions.
- Rules: It must move at the desire of the promisor. It may move from the promisee or *any other person* (Privity of Consideration is not strictly followed in India). It can be past, present, or future. It must be real and lawful, but it need not be 'adequate' (if you sell a 10 Lakh car for 1 Rupee with free consent, it is a valid contract).

core_concepts.title: Capacity to Contract (Section 11) & Minors
core_concepts.description:
Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority (18+), is of sound mind, and is not disqualified by law.
- Minor's Contract: An agreement with a minor is *Void Ab Initio* (void from the very beginning).
- Landmark Case: *Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903)* established that a minor's contract is absolutely void, and a minor cannot be forced to repay the money borrowed under a void contract (Rule of Estoppel does not apply to a minor).

core_concepts.title: Free Consent & Vitiating Factors (Sections 13-22)
core_concepts.description:
Consent is said to be free when it is not caused by:
1. Coercion (Sec 15): Committing or threatening to commit an act forbidden by the IPC (e.g., holding a gun to someone's head).
2. Undue Influence (Sec 16): Dominating the will of another using a fiduciary/active relationship (e.g., Doctor-Patient, Guru-Disciple).
3. Fraud (Sec 17): Intentional deception or active concealment of facts to cheat the other party.
4. Misrepresentation (Sec 18): Innocent, unintentional false statement of a fact.
5. Mistake (Sec 20-22): An erroneous belief about a matter of fact or law.

core_concepts.title: Void vs. Voidable Contracts
core_concepts.description:
- Voidable Contract [Sec 2(i)]: Enforceable at the option of the aggrieved party. (Contracts hit by Coercion, Undue Influence, Fraud, and Misrepresentation are Voidable. The victim can choose to cancel or continue).
- Void Agreement [Sec 2(g)]: Not enforceable by law. (Contracts hit by Bilateral Mistake of Fact, Minors, Unlawful object, or lack of Consideration are entirely Void).

important_entities.name: Exception to 'No Consideration, No Contract' (Sec 25)
important_entities.key_fact: A contract made out of natural love and affection is valid without consideration.
important_entities.significance: If an agreement is expressed in writing, registered, and made on account of natural love and affection between parties standing in a near relation to each other (e.g., Father gifting a house to his daughter), it is a valid contract even without consideration.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Mere silence as to facts likely to affect the willingness of a person to enter into a contract is NOT fraud (Caveat Emptor - Let the buyer beware). **Exception:** Silence is fraud ONLY when it is the 'duty of the person keeping silence to speak' (e.g., fiduciary relationships, insurance contracts) or when 'silence is equivalent to speech'.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: C U F M M (Coercion, Undue Influence, Fraud, Misrepresentation, Mistake)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Remember CUFMM. The first 4 make a contract Voidable. The last one (Bilateral Mistake of Fact) makes it Void.

exam_strategy_tips: If a CLAT or Judiciary question asks 'What is the nature of an agreement with a minor in India?', unconditionally select **Void Ab Initio (Void from the beginning)**, and cite the *Mohori Bibee* case if an explanation is required.
